title: Delhi Sultanate: the five dynasties and their monuments
seo_title: Delhi Sultanate: Five Dynasties, Rulers and Monuments
meta_description: The Delhi Sultanate, 1206 to 1526: the Mamluk, Khalji, Tughlaq, Sayyid and Lodi dynasties, key rulers, administration and the monuments left in Delhi.
summary: The Delhi Sultanate ruled from Delhi between 1206 and 1526 under five dynasties: the Mamluk (Slave), Khalji, Tughlaq, Sayyid and Lodi. It began with Qutbuddin Aibak and ended when Babur defeated Ibrahim Lodi at Panipat. Its rulers built the Qutb Minar, Siri, Tughlaqabad, Firozabad and the Lodi tombs.

paras: Muhammad of Ghor defeated Prithviraj Chauhan at the second battle of Tarain in 1192 and took Delhi soon after. When he died in 1206, his Turkish slave-commander Qutbuddin Aibak became independent ruler in north India. This is the conventional start date of the Delhi Sultanate.

Aibak began the Quwwat-ul-Islam mosque and the Qutb Minar on the site of the Chauhan citadel, now [the Qutb complex](the-qutb-complex.html). Inscriptions on the mosque say it was built with material from demolished temples, and carved temple pillars are still visible in its colonnades.

sections.h2: Key rulers and what to remember about them
list: Iltutmish (1211 to 1236): consolidated the Sultanate, received recognition from the Abbasid caliph, introduced the silver tanka and copper jital.
Raziya (1236 to 1240): the only woman to rule from Delhi in this period.
Balban (1266 to 1287): stressed royal prestige and harsh discipline, and organised defence against the Mongols.
Alauddin Khalji (1296 to 1316): repelled repeated Mongol invasions, sent campaigns to the Deccan and south under Malik Kafur, controlled market prices in Delhi and paid soldiers in cash.
Muhammad bin Tughlaq (1325 to 1351): moved much of the capital's elite to Daulatabad, issued token copper currency; both experiments were reversed.
Firoz Shah Tughlaq (1351 to 1388): built canals, towns and Firozabad, repaired older monuments and moved two Ashokan pillars to Delhi.
Timur's invasion (1398): sacked Delhi and weakened the Tughlaqs.
Sikandar Lodi (1489 to 1517): founded Agra as a base around 1504.
paras: Each ruler is easiest to remember with a building. Alauddin is the Alai Darwaza and the Siri walls; Muhammad bin Tughlaq is Jahanpanah and the [Bijay Mandal](bijay-mandal-the-city-of-jahanpanah.html); Firoz Shah is the madrasa at [Hauz Khas](hauz-khas.html).

sections.h2: Administration and society under the Sultanate
paras: The sultan ruled with the help of ministers such as the wazir (finance), the ariz-i-mamalik (army) and officials for religious affairs and justice. Land revenue was assigned to military commanders through the iqta system: an iqtadar collected revenue from a territory and maintained troops in return. Alauddin Khalji tightened revenue collection and measured land in the Doab.

Persian became the language of administration and court chronicles. Sufi orders, especially the Chishtis, became influential; the shrine of Nizamuddin Auliya, who lived through several reigns, is still active in Delhi. Architecture combined Central Asian forms like the true arch and dome with Indian building skills, the beginning of Indo-Islamic architecture.

sections.h2: Economy and trade under the Sultanate
paras: The Sultanate drew its wealth from land revenue in the Ganga-Yamuna Doab and from tribute and plunder in its campaigns. Delhi grew into one of the largest cities of the Islamic world. Ibn Battuta, the Moroccan traveller who served Muhammad bin Tughlaq as a judge in the 1330s and 1340s, described its markets, postal system and court in his account, the Rihla.

New techniques spread in this period. The spinning wheel and the cotton carder's bow are first well attested in north India around this time, and paper became more common. Firoz Shah Tughlaq's canals from the Yamuna and Sutlej carried water to new towns such as Hisar, where the [Firoz Shah palace complex](hisar-firoz-shah-palace-complex.html) still stands.

After Timur's raid, regional sultanates in Bengal, Jaunpur, Malwa, Gujarat and the Deccan became independent. The Lodis, Afghan rulers, held a reduced kingdom. In 1526 Babur, ruler of Kabul, defeated Ibrahim Lodi at the first battle of Panipat using field artillery and cavalry tactics, and the [Mughal empire](mughal-empire.html) began.

Almost every Sultanate dynasty left a city or major monument in Delhi, which is why the Sultanate is central to the story of the [seven cities of Delhi](seven-cities-of-delhi.html). A good sequence is the Qutb complex, [Tughlaqabad Fort](tughlaqabad-fort.html), Hauz Khas and [the Lodhi Garden monuments](lodhi-garden-monuments.html), which together cover all five dynasties.

faq.q: What are the five dynasties of the Delhi Sultanate?
faq.a: The Mamluk or Slave dynasty (1206 to 1290), the Khalji dynasty (1290 to 1320), the Tughlaq dynasty (1320 to 1414), the Sayyid dynasty (1414 to 1451) and the Lodi dynasty (1451 to 1526). Together they ruled from Delhi for 320 years.

faq.q: Who was the founder of the Delhi Sultanate?
faq.a: Qutbuddin Aibak, a Turkish slave-general of Muhammad of Ghor, is regarded as the founder. He became independent ruler in 1206 after Muhammad's death and began building the Qutb Minar and the Quwwat-ul-Islam mosque in Delhi.

faq.q: Why is it called the Slave dynasty?
faq.a: Several of its rulers, including Aibak, Iltutmish and Balban, began as military slaves (mamluks) before rising to power. Historians prefer the term Mamluk dynasty, or the early Turkish sultans, since the rulers were not all of one family.

The iqta was an assignment of land revenue from a territory to a military officer, the iqtadar or muqti. In return he kept troops and administered the area. Iqtas were transferable and not hereditary in principle, which helped the sultan control his nobles.

faq.q: Which Delhi Sultanate monuments can I visit in Delhi?
faq.a: Among many: the Qutb Minar and Alai Darwaza, Sultan Ghari, the walls of Siri, Tughlaqabad Fort and Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq's tomb, Begumpur mosque, Firoz Shah Kotla, the Hauz Khas complex, and the Sayyid and Lodi tombs in Lodhi Garden.

faq.q: Who was Alauddin Khalji and why is he important?
faq.a: Alauddin Khalji ruled from 1296 to 1316. He defeated repeated Mongol invasions, sent his general Malik Kafur on campaigns deep into the Deccan and south, built the city of Siri and the Alai Darwaza, and introduced market price controls and stricter land revenue collection in the Doab.

posts.hook: Delhi's Sultanate lasted 320 years under five dynasties.
posts.caption: Mamluk, Khalji, Tughlaq, Sayyid, Lodi. Every one of them left a monument you can still walk to in Delhi.

posts.hook: At the Qutb, look at the pillars, not just the minar.
posts.caption: The colonnades of the Quwwat-ul-Islam mosque reuse carved temple pillars, and the mosque's own inscription says so. It is a lesson in how monuments record history.
